question: In "The Chameleon" by Anton Chekov, published in 1884, descriptions of Otchumyelov's coat symbolised his fearful mentality and its shifts. How many times did Chekov describe the coat?

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: In the text as it is normally printed the inspector Ochumelov/Ochumyelov's outer garment is not a constant scenic property, it is a rhetorical marker. In the Garnett/standard English version and in the Russian original the sheepskin / greatcoat / overcoat is called up only as a way of registering a change in Ochumelov's internal colour.

The first registration is the establishing registration of the man in the street: the police
captain is out in his winter sheepskin / coat and is comfortably superior to the crowd and to the bitten dog. The garment is then re-mentioned the first time his colour changes, when he begins to pull himself together and to show off in front of the crowd and of the potential General-owner of the dog, and it is re-mentioned a third time when he has completed the reversal and is again swaggering / cringing. That is the three-stage chameleon movement of the story – confident superiority → fearful self-abasement → renewed swagger – which the garment is made to carry. 

In a literal word-count the Russian шинель/шуба/пальто and the English “overcoat/shee- 
pskin coat” are hit four times in the short sketch, the fourth hit being the reprise of the third descriptive state. The three descriptive states are the ones normally quoted as the symbolic shifts of the coat.

Then, as his anxiety grows and he tries to placate the crowd, the coat is noted as being rumpled and his buttons are fumbled, showing the loss of composure. Finally, when he decides to side with the higher-ups and the mood turns again, the coat is described a last time as he straightens it and tries to regain authority, the shift in the description mirroring his final craven reversal. Those three descriptive beats track the chameleon-like change in mentality.
